« Où sont les parents ? » Voilà une ques: “Where are the parents?” It’s a question that has been heard many times in the wake of gun violence incidents involving young people. That question has serious repercussions for young people, but also for those around them.
Si les parents sont directement touchés: While parents are directly affected by the problems their teenagers face, the measures put in place to prevent these incidents often exclude them. In Montréal, immigrant parents experience this form of exclusion more acutely.
Face à des parents bouleversés, choqués: Faced with parents who are distraught, shocked or even grieving, everyone is calling for solutions — in coordination with them, not in spite of them. To better understand why parents are being left out, La Converse looked into the consequences of isolating families when young people end up caught up in violent, sometimes bloody, incidents.
<l1>Dans une récente étude québécoise</l: <l1>In a recent Quebec study</l1>, experts in juvenile delinquency argue that Quebec’s youth protection system is oriented solely toward the child — which implies a shortfall when it comes to parental responsibility. In Quebec, the approach to youth protection therefore focuses on young people, often leaving behind the parents and families of young offenders.
Ayant travaillé à la Direction de la pro: Having worked at the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ) for more than 10 years, Myriam Coppry saw that there was very little or no room for parents in the process of prevention and in the measures meant to help young people. “Parents desperately need help,” she says right off the bat. To make up for the lack of resources for them, in 2020 she founded NunanuQ, a multidisciplinary parent coaching service that helps parents in intercultural contexts.
« Malheureusement, lorsque les parents v: “Unfortunately, when parents come to us for help, they’re already at the end of their rope. The damage has already been done,” the parent coaching expert exclaims. Out of solutions, these parents only realize how serious the situation is when the police or the DPJ step in. “We downplay it, we don’t realize our child could have gone that far. Then we start questioning ourselves. Where did we miss that there were problems? Did we do a bad job passing on our values?” she asks, herself a mother and grandmother.
Pour les parents issus de l’immigration,: For immigrant parents, raising a child in a country they didn’t know growing up remains one of the greatest challenges there is. M<sup>s</sup> Coppry mentions it several times: “No one has been trained to raise a child in the unknown.” Here, an understanding of intercultural issues is key to understanding and assisting parents whose young people are experiencing violence.
La fondatrice de NunanuQ explique qu’il: NunanuQ’s founder explains that there are various reasons why immigrant parents are, from the very start, cut off from the problems affecting their children. “When a child grows up in an environment completely different from their parents’, they behave differently at home and outside. So the parent can’t know who their child is outside the home, since there are often different sociocultural codes for the young person depending on where they are,” she says.
À toutes les problématiques déjà présent: On top of all the problems outlined above come challenges specific to immigrant parents. “We know that the way the community looks at you plays a big role; parents are often afraid to seek help because they’re not familiar with the Quebec system. That adds an extra layer between the parent and institutions like the DPJ, for example,” she explains.
M<sup>me</sup> Coppry a pu constater au: Over the years, M<sup>s</sup> Coppry has seen the harm that parents’ absence has done to young people. “I’ve seen intervention plans signed without the parents even knowing. How can a young person grow and develop if their parents don’t even know about the difficulties they have to overcome?” she asks.
Aujourd’hui, les jeunes sont en contact: Today, young people are coming into contact with gun violence earlier and earlier. <l1>While it has decreased in Montréal over the past two years, this form of violence has nonetheless affected more minors</l1> and, therefore, more parents and families.
<strong>Traiter le problème à la racine<: Getting to the root of the problem
« Être une personne à la maison et en êt: “Being one person at home and another outside is everyday life for a lot of immigrant children,” Myriam Coppry repeated several times. It is also one of the symptoms of the disconnect between these parents and their children, who are growing up far from the land where their parents were born.
Pour Rola Koubeissy, professeure adjoint: For Rola Koubeissy, an assistant professor at Université de Montréal who specializes in learning in contexts of diversity and inclusion among young people and their families, there are several issues tied to the healthy integration of young immigrants. “The most important ones,” she says over the phone, “are above all the cultural and social issues. It’s hard to feel that you belong in your host society.”
Elle insiste sur le fait que le renforce: She stresses that strengthening this sense of belonging has to happen through institutions, especially schools. “It’s at school that young people need to feel included, to understand that they have their place here, even if they weren’t born here, or their parents weren’t born here. If these issues aren’t taken into account, that’s where we’ll create discrimination and marginalization against these children,” she emphasizes.
L’un des points faibles de l’intégration: One of the weak points in these young people’s integration is that not enough emphasis is placed on parental involvement, the university instructor believes. “When we don’t know how to involve parents in their children’s lives, we add to the divide that exists between them, but also between parents and institutions.”
<strong>Qu’est-ce qui isole les parents: What isolates immigrant parents from their kids’ lives?
Il est facile de tomber dans les préjugé: It’s easy to fall into prejudice. M<sup>s</sup> Koubeissy points this out, explaining that “we shouldn’t assume parents are uninterested because they’re not familiar with Quebec culture or the Quebec system. They came here so their loved ones could succeed, and despite the differences, they share a common goal with the other people involved in their kids’ lives.”
L’experte en psychopédagogie trouve qu’i: The educational psychology expert also finds that there is a lack of concrete means to facilitate dialogue between parents and institutions. “Minimal communication isn’t enough. We need to create options for engagement, interest and involvement so that parents know what’s going on with the students. Not only does this support students’ learning and integration, it also allows parents to be on the same wavelength as their kids, to understand them better,” she concludes.
